problem: Robot learning models are mostly task- or hardware-specific and need redesign and retraining per task. Prior robot representation learning mostly uses perception only and treats dynamics separately, and there is no shared pretrained representation for a robot that serves several tasks.
motivation: Large pretrained models in language and vision provide a general starting point for many tasks. Robotics data is expensive and scarce, and real-time compute is limited, so one shared expensive backbone with lightweight task heads would be attractive. The paper observes that robots share a perception-action loop, so modeling state-action transitions should yield a general robot-specific representation.
key_idea: Pretrain a GPT-style causal transformer on interleaved state (observation) and action tokens with autoregressive next-action and next-state-token prediction, then reuse it, frozen or finetuned, with small heads for localization, mapping and navigation.
insight: Joint state and action prediction gives richer representations than either alone (Table pretext: on MuSHR, localization ATE is 52.0 with state-only, 4.34 with action-only and 4.21 with both; on Habitat, 2.92, 3.218 and 1.512). A pretrained backbone helps most in low-data regimes and for joint multi-head training (Table joint: MuSHR 100 episodes, ATE 18.5 from scratch vs 10.3). Given enough data, training from scratch can catch up or surpass it (Habitat mapping, Fig. speed). Bigger models predict actions better offline but crash earlier in deployment because of inference latency.
method: Tokenizers: separate per-modality tokenizers. RGB uses a ResNet-18 trained from scratch giving a 128-d token. LiDAR uses PointNet without transform blocks, or a 200x200 BEV image through ResNet-18 (more robust for sim-to-real). Discrete actions use a linear embedding and continuous actions a 2-layer MLP.
Causal transformer: GPT-like, 12 layers, 8 heads, 128-d embedding. It takes K=16 timesteps as 2K alternating state/action tokens, with global and local time embeddings as in Decision Transformer.

Pretraining objectives: self-supervised. The action head h_a predicts a_t from the state embedding (policy). The state head h_s predicts the next state token q(s_{t+1}) from the state and action embeddings (dynamics).

Localization head: 3-layer MLP [64,32,3] on the previous state and action embeddings plus the current state embedding. It predicts the pose delta (dX, dY, dtheta) with MSE, and deltas are integrated over time with a rolling window.
Mapping head: 2-layer deconvolutional decoder outputting a 64x64 local occupancy image covering 15x15 m, from the K-step history embeddings, trained with MSE.
Downstream regimes: the transformer is either frozen (F, only the head is trained) or fully trainable (T), compared with the same architecture from random init and with joint multi-head training.
Data: MuSHR simulator on an office map with an MPC expert, 5.5K trajectories (3M tokens). Habitat PointNav expert trajectories, 10K episodes (840K tokens).

setting.backbone: 12-layer causal transformer (GPT-like) with ResNet-18 / PointNet tokenizers, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Self-supervised pretraining on expert trajectories: 5.5K MuSHR simulated LiDAR trajectories (3M tokens) and 10K Habitat PointNav episodes (840K tokens); downstream heads finetuned on the same data
setting.observation: 2D LiDAR scans (MuSHR) or first-person RGB 224x224 (Habitat) plus past actions
setting.action_space: MuSHR: continuous steering angle [-21.75, 21.75] deg; Habitat: discrete left/right/forward/stop
setting.simulator: MuSHR simulator (real office map) and Habitat
setting.privileged: none (ground-truth pose deltas and occupancy maps are used only as training labels for the heads)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark (R2R, ObjectNav, etc.) is evaluated. The results are localization ATE and mapping MSE on the authors' own MuSHR and Habitat data, so none are listed as benchmark numbers.
results: PACT-initialized models match or beat scratch models in most cases. In joint multi-head training with a PACT representation, MuSHR ATE at 100 episodes is 10.3 vs 18.5 from scratch, and Habitat ATE at 800 episodes is 0.802 vs 1.233. Fully trainable scratch networks sometimes win with abundant data (MuSHR ATE at 5500 episodes: 3.08 scratch-T vs 3.62 PACT-T). The pretrained model also showed prompt-conditioned action generation and about 80 m runs in a real-world MuSHR deployment.
limitations: Evaluated only on small, self-generated simulated datasets and two robot platforms. No standard navigation benchmarks or comparison to other robot pretraining methods.
With enough finetuning data, training from scratch often matches or exceeds PACT; the gains concentrate in low-data regimes.
Real-world testing is qualitative, with runs up to about 80 m and no quantitative sim-to-real evaluation. Larger models suffer from inference latency.
compares_to: Same architecture trained from scratch (Scratch F/T)
